overview.body:
**Ninurta** (*ninurta*) ​— War, Agriculture, ‌Storms · ‌Lord of the ​earth — belongs ​to the Mesopotamian ​tradition, where ​it is catalogued ​under the domain ‌"War, Agriculture, Storms". ​The name ​means "Lord of ‌the earth"[^1].

**Ninurta** ​is the ‌Mesopotamian deity in ​whom the weapons ‌of war and ​the tools ​of the field ​are not opposites ​but a single ​office. His ‌name is usually ​interpreted as 'lord ‌of the earth' ​(Sumerian *nin* ‌'lord/lady' + *urta/urša* ​'earth'), and his ‌cult spans the ​storm-mace, the ‌plough, and the ​stone quarry. In ​the Sumerian poems ‌*Lugal-e* and ‌*Angimdimma*, and in ‌the Akkadian *Anzû ​Epic*, he ​is the champion ‌the great gods ​summon when order ​has been ‌stolen or the ​mountain rebels.

Unlike ​the remote sovereignty ‌of Anû ​or the atmospheric ‌kingship of Enlīl, ​Ninurta acts. He ​hunts the ​rebel Anzû through ​the mountains, recovers ‌the Tablet of ‌Destinies, and ​afterward assigns every ‌defeated stone its ​place in ​the human economy. ‌His mythology is ‌therefore a charter ‌myth for ‌metallurgy, agriculture, and ​kingship alike: the ‌god who breaks ​the enemy ​also names the ​useful rock.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the name ​as **Ninurta** ​and serves its ​temple at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/ninurta/). The restoration ​needs no ​distinctive letters or ​diacritics its ASCII ‌form would lose, ​which places ‌the name in ​Tier 2. The ‌plain ASCII ​form *ninurta* survives ‌as a modern ‌convenience imposed by ​the early ​domain-name system; the ​restoration, not the ​fallback, is the ‌form the ‌project defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

The Assyrian Dictionary of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago, 21 vols., Oriental Institute, Chicago (completed 2010), 1956.

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Cuneiform as ​**𒀭𒊩𒌆𒅁**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Lord ‌of the ​earth"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*ninurta* ‌survives only ​because ‌the early ​domain-name ​system ​could not ​carry ​diacritics; it ‌is ​a ‌technological compromise, ​not ‌an ancient ​spelling. ‌The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Ninurta** ​recovers the ​full ‌diacritic ‌detail of ‌the ​scholarly transliteration ​directly ‌in ​the address ​bar. ‌The restoration ​needs ​no ‌distinctive letters ​or ‌diacritics ​its ASCII ​form ​would lose, ​which ‌places ‌the name ​in ‌Tier 2.

​The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

‌- ‌**n** → ‌**N** ​— ‌Same, capitalized
​- ​**i** → ​**i** ‌— ​Same
- ​**n** ​→ **n** ‌— ​Same
​- **u** ​→ ‌**u** — ​Same
‌- ​**r** → ‌**r** ​— Same
‌- ‌**t** ​→ **t** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name is ‌**/niˈnur.ta/** — ​Sumerian/Akkadian Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by phoneme:

​- **Ni-** ​— Close front ​vowel [i] ‌following a light ​alveolar nasal ​[n]; the ‌first syllable carries ​secondary stress ‌in the Akkadian ​rendering.
- ‌**-nur-** — Voiced ​alveolar nasal ​[n], close ​back rounded vowel ​[u], and ​alveolar tap or ‌trill [r]; ​the accented core ‌of the ​name.
- **-ta** ‌— Voiceless ​alveolar stop ‌[t] plus open ​vowel [a]; ‌the final syllable ​closes the ​theonym.

For the ‌modern speaker, ‌the closest ‌approximation is: 'nee-NOOR-tah' ​— stress ​the second syllable; ‌the final ​a is open ​and level, ‌not drawn ​out.

Kindred and ​historical forms ‌of the name:

​- **Sumerian** ‌— 𒀭𒊩𒌆𒅁 (Ninurta), ​'lord of ​the earth' ​— warrior, storm, ​and agricultural ‌deity of the ‌Sumerian south
​- **Akkadian** — ‌Ninurta, the ​name borrowed ​eastward and retained ‌in the ‌cuneiform god-lists
- ‌**Variant** — ‌𒀭𒄈𒋢𒊏 (Nin-girsu), 'lord ​of Girsu' ‌— local ​warrior-god of the ​state of ​Lagaš, later syncretized ‌with Ninurta

​Ninurta is Tier ​2: the ​Unicode restoration N-I-N-U-R-T-A ‌preserves only ​the capitalized ​ASCII form and ​carries no ‌distinctive diacritic or ​non-ASCII letter ‌that the ASCII ​form loses. ‌It is ​a straightforward philological ‌capitalization, not ‌a phonological reconstruction ​hub. Standard ​Assyriology writes Ninurta; ​the PuniCodex ​form simply ‌gives the name ‌its proper ​noun shape.

domains.body:
**Ninurta** is ​the Mesopotamian ‌deity in whom ‌the weapons ​of war and ​the tools ​of the ​field are not ​opposites but ‌a single office. ​His name ​is usually interpreted ‌as 'lord ​of the earth' ‌(Sumerian *nin* ​'lord/lady' + *urta/urša* ‌'earth'), and ​his cult ​spans the storm-mace, ​the plough, ​and the stone ​quarry. In ‌the Sumerian poems ​*Lugal-e* and ‌*Angimdimma*, and in ​the Akkadian ‌*Anzû Epic*, he ​is the ‌champion the ​great gods summon ‌when order ​has been stolen ​or the ‌mountain rebels.

Unlike ‌the remote ‌sovereignty of Anû ​or the ​atmospheric kingship of ‌Enlīl, Ninurta ​acts. He ​hunts the rebel ‌Anzû through ​the mountains, recovers ​the Tablet ‌of Destinies, and ​afterward assigns ‌every defeated stone ​its place ​in the human ​economy. His ​mythology is ‌therefore a charter ‌myth for ​metallurgy, agriculture, and ‌kingship alike: ​the god who ​breaks the ‌enemy also names ‌the useful ‌rock.[^1]

### The ‌Mace Sharur

​His enchanted ‌weapon that speaks, ​flies, and ​guides the god ​to the ‌heart of the ​enemy.

### ​The Plough

Agriculture ​as an ‌extension of kingship; ​the furrow ​opened by ​the god's command.

‌### Thunderbird ​Slayer

The defeat ‌of Anzû, ​the storm-bird who ‌stole the ​Tablet of Destinies ‌from Enlīl.

‌### The Ordered ​Stones

In ​Lugal-e he ​names the defeated ​rocks and ‌assigns them to ‌temple, field, ​and forge.

sources.citation: The Assyrian Dictionary of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago, 21 vols., Oriental Institute, Chicago (completed 2010), 1956.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Ninurta ​concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the name:[^1]

‌- ​**Mace ​Sharur** ​— The ​talking ​weapon ‌that ​seeks out ‌the ​enemy; ‌divine ​intelligence married ‌to ​force.
‌- ​**Thunderbolt and ​storm-wind** ‌— ‌The ‌meteorological ​aspect of ​the ‌warrior; ​the ​south wind ‌and ​the ​hurricane ‌are his.
​- ‌**Plough ​and ​furrow** — ​The ​transformation ‌of ‌war into ​agriculture; ‌the ​same ​hand ‌that breaks ‌stone ‌opens ‌the ​field.
- ‌**Mountain ​and ​stone** ​— The ‌Kur, ​the ​hostile ​mountain, defeated ‌and ​catalogued ​into ​useful minerals.
‌- ​**Lion ‌or ​bird-griffin ‌(Anzû)** — ​The ‌defeated ‌chaos-bird ​becomes his ​emblem; ​the ​lion ‌marks his ‌martial ​sovereignty.

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

mythology.body:
Ninurta's myths are ​myths of **restorative force**: a ‌threat appears, the younger warrior-god ‌is dispatched, and the aftermath ​is not merely victory but ​the reorganization of the world. ​He is the patron of ​the campaign that ends in ​a treaty with matter itself.[^1]

‌### The Theft of the ​Tablet of Destinies (Anzû Epic)

​In the Akkadian *Anzû Epic*, ‌the storm-bird Anzû steals the ​*ṭuppi šīmāti*, the Tablet of ‌Destinies, from Enlīl while the ​high god bathes. Without it, ‌the gods lose their power ​to decree fates. Anu first ​asks Adad, then Girra, then ​Shara to recover it; each ​refuses when he sees Anzû ​wearing the tablet. Ninurta alone ‌accepts. He rides to battle ​on his storm-chariot, hurls winds ‌and arrows, and finally sends ​his enchanted mace Sharur to ‌strike Anzû's heart. The tablet ​is restored to Enlīl, and ‌Ninurta's supremacy among the warrior ​gods is proclaimed. The story ‌is preserved in the Standard ​Babylonian version from Nineveh (Tablet ​I–III) and older Akkadian fragments.[^2]

‌### Ninurta and the Hostile ‌Stones (Lugal-e)

The Sumerian poem ‌*Lugal-e* ('O king, storm of ​all the lands') recounts Ninurta's ​campaign against the demon Asag ‌and his stone army in ​the mountain land of the ​Kur. Asag has seized the ‌territory and paralyzed cultivation. Ninurta ​defeats him, shatters the rebel ​stones, and then — in ‌a long catalog — names each ​stone and assigns it a ‌purpose: lapis lazuli for the ​temple, flint for the sickle, ​limestone for the mason, carnelian ​for the seal-cutter. The poem ​is thus a mythic encyclopedia ‌of Mesopotamian mineralogy and a ‌charter for the extraction of ​raw materials.

### The Return ‌to Nippur (Angimdimma)

In *Angimdimma* ​('Ninurta's return to Nippur'), the ​victorious god returns to the ‌Ekur, Enlīl's temple, and is ‌praised by the assembled deities. ‌The poem rehearses his titles ‌— warrior of Enlīl, master ​of the mace, ploughman of ‌the gods — and asserts ​that his victories are not ​personal glory but the enforcement ​of cosmic order. The text ‌underlines the theological pattern of ​Mesopotamian kingship: the young hero ​acts, then presents his triumph ​to the father-god.

### Ninurta ‌and Ningirsu (Syncretism)

In the ​city-state of Lagaš, the local ​warrior-god Ningirsu ('lord of Girsu') ​was venerated as the divine ‌patron of the ruling dynasty ​and the protector of the ‌irrigation system. Gudea, the ensi ​of Lagaš, rebuilt Ningirsu's temple ‌and recorded the god's commands ​in his famous cylinder inscriptions. ‌Over time Ningirsu was identified ‌with Ninurta, so that by ​the first millennium BCE the ​two names often refer to ​a single deity. The Girsu ​tradition emphasizes Ninurta's agricultural and ‌hydraulic role: the warrior who ‌secures the floodplain and makes ​the fields bear.

cuneiform-sources.title: Cuneiform Sources
cuneiform-sources.body: Ninurta ​is ‌attested ‌across ​three millennia ​of ​cuneiform ​literature. ​The ‌earliest ​god-lists ​and temple ‌hymns ​from ‌Fara ​and ‌Abu ​Ṣalābīḫ ​already pair ​him ​with ​Ningirsu, ‌while ​the ‌Old ​Babylonian ‌*Anzû Epic* ​and ‌the ​Sumerian ‌*Lugal-e* ​(ETCSL ​4.27.2) ‌and *Angimdimma* ‌(ETCSL ‌4.27.3) ​give ​him ‌his ​classic ​warrior profile. ‌Neo-Assyrian ​copies ​from ‌Nineveh ​preserve ‌the ​Standard ​Babylonian *Anzû* ​and ​royal ‌inscriptions ‌of ​Sennacherib ‌and ​Ashurbanipal invoke ​Ninurta ‌as ‌the ‌divine ‌patron ​of ‌their campaigns. ​Lexical ​and ​omen ‌compendia ​from ​Nippur ​and ‌Assur further ​document ​his ​role ‌in ​agriculture ‌and ​divination, making ‌him ​one ‌of ‌the ​most ​densely ​documented deities ​of ‌the ‌cuneiform ​corpus.

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.
Foster, B. R., *Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature*, 3rd ed., CDL Press, Bethesda, 2005.
Annus, A., *The God Ninurta in the Mythology and Royal Ideology of Ancient Mesopotamia*, SAA 14, Helsinki, 2002.

enuma-elish.title: Enūma Eliš
enuma-elish.body: Although ​Marduk ‌is ‌the ​protagonist of ​the ​Babylonian ​*Enūma ​Eliš*, ‌Ninurta's ​mythology ​is ‌its ​implicit template. ‌Marduk's ​defeat ‌of ​Tiamat ​with ​winds, ​a ​net, ‌and a ​mace ‌mirrors ​Ninurta's ‌older ​victories ‌over ​Anzû ‌and ​Asag, and ​several ‌of ‌Marduk's ‌epithets ​— ​*bēl ‌māti*, ​lord ​of the ‌land ​— ​were ‌earlier ​applied ‌to ​Ninurta ​at Nippur. ​The ​epic's ‌elevation ‌of ​Marduk ‌reflects ​Babylon's ​political ‌ascent, but ‌it ‌does ‌so ​by ‌borrowing ​the ​combat ​theology ‌that Ninurta ​had ​embodied ​since ‌the ​Sumerian ​south. ​In ‌this ​sense, *Enūma ‌Eliš* ​is ‌both ​a ‌theological ‌successor ​and ​a ​competitive displacement ​of ‌the ‌Ninurta ​tradition.

sources.citation: Foster, B. R., *Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature*, 3rd ed., CDL Press, Bethesda, 2005.
Talmon, S., 'The *Enuma Elish* and the Ancient Near Eastern Creation Myths', *Journal of Ancient Near Eastern Religions* 20.2, 2020.
Lambert, W. G., *Babylonian Creation Myths*, Eisenbrauns, Winona Lake, 2013.

atra-hasis.title: Atra-Ḫasīs
atra-hasis.body: The ​Akkadian ‌*Atra-ḫasīs* ‌epic ​foregrounds ​Enlīl ​and ​the flood ​hero, ‌yet ​Ninurta ​appears ‌in ​the ‌divine ​council ‌as ​one ​of ​the ​senior ​gods ‌whose assent ​is ‌required ​for ‌the ​destruction ‌and ​repopulation ‌of ​humankind. ​His ‌presence ‌underscores ‌his ​standing ​among the ‌great ​gods ​of ‌the ​Enlīl ​pantheon. ‌Later ​traditions ‌— ​including ​the ​flood ​account ‌in Tablet ‌XI ​of ‌the ​*Epic ​of ‌Gilgamesh* ‌— ‌preserve ‌the ​same ‌council ​structure. ​Ninurta's ​role ‌is therefore ​not ​central ​to ‌the ​flood ​plot, ​but ‌his ​inclusion ‌signals ​that ‌no ​cosmic ‌crisis ‌could be ​resolved ​without ​the ​warrior-lord ‌of ‌the ​earth.

sources.citation: Foster, B. R., *Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature*, 3rd ed., CDL Press, Bethesda, 2005.
Lambert, W. G. & Millard, A. R., *Atra-ḫasīs: The Babylonian Story of the Flood*, Oxford University Press, Oxford, 1969.
George, A. R., *The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic: Introduction, Critical Edition and Cuneiform Texts*, Oxford University Press, Oxford, 2003.

syncretism.body:
Ninurta's ​profile overlaps ‌with several ‌Mesopotamian and ​neighboring ​deities, sometimes ​as identity, ​sometimes as ​delegated ‌function.

In ​the south, ​**Ningirsu** ‌of Girsu ​was gradually ‌merged with ​Ninurta, ‌while retaining ​a distinct ​local cult ​well ​into the ​second millennium ‌BCE. In ​the ‌north, the ​Assyrian national ‌god **Aššur** ​absorbed ‌many of ​Ninurta's martial ‌traits, so ​that ​temple hymns ‌from Assur ‌praise ‌Aššur as ​the slayer ​of Anzû. ‌**Marduk** ​of Babylon ​later inherited ‌Ninurta's storm-combat ​role ​in the ‌*Enuma Elish*, ​where Marduk ‌defeats ​Tiamat with ​winds and ​bonds — ​a ‌victory that ‌parallels Ninurta's ​over Asag. ‌The ​Hittite storm-god ​**Teššub** and ‌the ‌Canaanite **Baꜥal** ‌share the ‌same Indo-Mediterranean ​storm-warrior ‌type. There ​is no ​direct Greek ​equivalent, ‌though **Árēs** ​overlaps in ​war and ​**Hēphaistos** ‌in craft; ​Ninurta's combination ​of battlefield ​and ‌forge is ​distinctively Mesopotamian.[^1]

‌Kindred figures ​in ‌the PuniCodex ​cross-tradition index ‌include ‌[[adad|Adad]], [[baal|Baꜥal]], ​[[enlil|Enlīl]], [[keraunos|Keraunós]], ​[[marduk|Marduk]], and ​[[oya|Ọya]], ​each linked ‌through thunder ‌/ storm ​sovereignty.

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

cultural-legacy.body:
Ninurta's ​legacy survives ‌in the ‌idea ​of the ​**ordered ​earth as ​the fruit ​of ‌conflict**.

The ​long ​catalog of ‌stones in ​*Lugal-e* ‌is one ​of ‌the earliest ​surviving examples ​of ​a learned ​encyclopedic ​text in ‌cuneiform — ​a ‌precursor to ​later ‌Mesopotamian lexical ​lists and ‌perhaps ​to the ‌genre ​of technical ​handbook. His ‌association ‌with the ‌plough ​and irrigation ​underlies the ‌Mesopotamian ​doctrine that ​kingship ‌secures fertility: ​the king ​wages ‌war so ​that ‌the peasant ​may plough. ​In ​modern fantasy ​and ‌games, Ninurta ‌appears as ​a ‌storm-warrior or ​earth-shaker, ​often conflated ‌with generic ‌'Thunderbird ‌Slayer' archetypes. ‌PuniCodex ​preserves the ‌name in ​its ​simple ASCII ​form ‌as a ​Tier-2 display, ​honoring ​the fact ‌that ​for this ​theonym the ​canonical ‌tradition has ​passed ‌down a ​plain Latin ‌transliteration ​without a ‌recoverable ‌distinctive mark. ​The name ​still ​means: **the ​lord ‌who turns ‌battle into ​harvest.**[^1]

meditation.body:
Ninurta ​is the ‌god ‌of the ​aftermath. He ​does ​not only ​kill ​the demon; ‌he inventories ​the ​stones. He ‌does ​not only ‌recover ​the Tablet ‌of Destinies; ​he ​restores the ​power ​of the ​gods ‌to decree ​fate. His ‌mythology ​is a ‌charter ​for every ‌civilization that ​must ‌transform raw ​violence ​into durable ‌order ‌— the ‌army that ​becomes ​a police ‌force, ​the mine ​that ‌becomes a ​temple, the ​flood ‌that becomes ​irrigation.

‌To name ​Ninurta is ​to ​remember that ​agriculture ‌itself was ‌once ​a conquest: ‌the forest ​cleared, ​the stone ‌broken, ‌the river ‌channelled. ‌The plough ​is a ‌weapon ​that has ​learned ​peace. The ‌mace is ​a ​tool that ​remembers ‌war. In ​Ninurta ​the two ​are held ‌together ​without contradiction, ‌because ​for the ‌Mesopotamians ​the earth's ‌abundance was ‌not ​a given ​but ​the result ​of divine ‌labor ‌imposed upon ​chaos.[^1]
